title: Genre, conventions and comparison
summary: Genres are sets of expectations that writers follow, bend or break. Understanding conventions lets you compare texts and works meaningfully.

keyterms.definition: A category of texts sharing conventions of form, content and purpose, e.g. tragedy, sonnet, editorial, advert.
An expected feature of a genre or text type, such as a headline in a news report or a volta in a sonnet.
Deliberately breaking or overturning a convention or expectation to create meaning.
A text that blends the conventions of two or more genres or text types.
The shape and structure of a text, such as sonnet, free verse, letter or graphic novel.
Analysing similarities and differences between texts to show how each creates meaning.
A specific shared idea, technique or feature used to organise a comparative argument.
A dramatic genre in which a protagonist's downfall, often linked to a flaw, arouses pity and fear.
A novel of formation that follows a protagonist's growth from youth to maturity.
A genre imagining an oppressive society, used to warn about present tendencies.

questions.prompt: Which is a convention of a hard news report?
options: The most important facts in the opening paragraph
questions.explanation: News reports typically front-load key facts (the inverted pyramid) so readers grasp the story quickly.

questions.text: Deliberately breaking a genre's expected features to create meaning is called ___.
questions.explanation: Subversion works only because readers know the convention being broken.

questions.prompt: Match the genre to a typical convention.
questions.explanation: Knowing conventions helps you spot where a text conforms or deviates.

questions.statement: A charity advert that looks like a luxury fashion advert until you read the small print is an example of a hybrid or subversive text.
questions.explanation: Borrowing and then overturning a genre's conventions creates surprise and sharpens the message.

questions.prompt: A recipe written as a love poem is best described as:
questions.explanation: It blends the conventions of instructions and lyric poetry; ask what the blend achieves.

questions.text: The shape and structure of a text, such as free verse or a letter, is its ___.
questions.explanation: Form shapes meaning: a poem in the form of a list feels different from one in sonnet form.

questions.prompt: A dystopian novel shows citizens rated on their every purchase. What is its likely purpose?
options: To warn about trends in present-day society
questions.explanation: Dystopias exaggerate present tendencies to make readers question them.

questions.statement: Genres are fixed and never change over time.
questions.explanation: Genres evolve as writers innovate and as media change (e.g. the blog, the podcast, the tweet thread).

questions.prompt: Why is naming the genre of an unseen text useful in Paper 1?
options: It earns a mark on its own
It lets you discuss how the text uses or departs from expected conventions for its audience
It tells you the author's name
questions.explanation: Genre awareness is useful only when linked to how conventions create effects.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of the inverted-pyramid news structure, top to bottom.
items: Lead paragraph with who, what, when, where
questions.explanation: Editors can cut from the bottom without losing the core story.

questions.prompt: Which essay structure is usually strongest for comparison?
options: All of work A, then all of work B
Paragraphs organised by points of comparison, discussing both works in each
Only discussing the more interesting work
questions.explanation: Integrated comparison keeps both works in dialogue and sustains focus on the question.

questions.text: A shared idea or technique used to organise a comparative paragraph is a point of ___.
questions.explanation: Good points of comparison allow both similarities and differences to emerge.

questions.prompt: Match the connective to its comparative function.
questions.explanation: Precise connectives make comparative thinking visible to the examiner.

questions.statement: Good comparison discusses differences as well as similarities.
questions.explanation: Differences in method or perspective often produce the most insightful comparisons.

questions.prompt: Two novels both explore exile: one through a single narrator's memories, the other through alternating voices. What is the most productive comparison?
options: How narrative structure shapes each work's sense of exile as private or collective
questions.explanation: Comparing how form shapes meaning addresses both what and how, which examiners reward.

options: Text A uses imagery. Text B uses imagery too.
While both texts use storm imagery, Text A makes it a threat to the community, whereas Text B treats it as cleansing renewal.
Text A is better than Text B.
I will now talk about Text B.
questions.explanation: It identifies a shared feature and then sharpens the difference in effect.

questions.text: A novel tracing a young protagonist's growth to maturity is a ___.
questions.explanation: Coming-of-age novels often explore identity, which makes them good comparison partners.

questions.statement: In a comparison, the two works must be from the same genre.
questions.explanation: Works in different genres can be compared fruitfully; differences in form can be a point of comparison.

questions.prompt: What should a comparative conclusion do?
options: Repeat each paragraph word for word
Synthesise how the two works answer the question differently and why that matters
Apologise for running out of time
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion draws the comparison together into a final judgement.

questions.prompt: In a tragedy, what does the protagonist's downfall typically arouse in the audience?
questions.explanation: Since Aristotle, tragedy has been associated with pity and fear and the release of catharsis.
